<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="MEDLINE" Owner="NLM" IndexingMethod="Manual"><PMID Version="1">30883276</PMID><DateCompleted><Year>2019</Year><Month>12</Month><Day>09</Day></DateCompleted><DateRevised><Year>2019</Year><Month>12</Month><Day>17</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Print-Electronic"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Electronic">1530-888X</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Internet"><Volume>31</Volume><Issue>5</Issue><PubDate><Year>2019</Year><Month>May</Month></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Neural computation</Title><ISOAbbreviation>Neural Comput</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>Sparse Associative Memory.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>998</StartPage><EndPage>1014</EndPage><MedlinePgn>998-1014</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1162/neco_a_01181</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>It is still unknown how associative biological memories operate. Hopfield networks are popular models of associative memory, but they suffer from spurious memories and low efficiency. Here, we present a new model of an associative memory that overcomes these deficiencies. We call this model sparse associative memory (SAM) because it is based on sparse projections from neural patterns to pattern-specific neurons. These sparse projections have been shown to be sufficient to uniquely encode a neural pattern. Based on this principle, we investigate theoretically and in simulation our SAM model, which turns out to have high memory efficiency and a vanishingly small probability of spurious memories. This model may serve as a basic building block of brain functions involving associative memory.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author
